utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only a small matter but I guess it is better to get rid of that early on in the morning. You have requested that we check which documents were tendered earlier and which possibly not, so to make a cross reference on the numbers, and we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think as a matter of principle, we should work on the Z numbers, the original numbers. So for the purposes of judgement and submissions and things, those will be the governing numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as a general rule, if we have confusion or double numbering sometimes, Z number is prevailing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the question of exhibits, I think Mr. Kovacic has also satisfied himself that D87/2, the document of the 24th of April that he produced yesterday and relied on in relation to troop positions and the map was not a document that had been produced in the Blaskic case, but it is a document that has come into his possession more recently and from elsewhere. It's a recent document. I don't know that he's exactly tied down yet where it came from, but it's not a Blaskic production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, just as a matter of reference, in order to have an absolutely clear record, we were trying to find out the source exactly. Yesterday I was under the impression that the document was used in Blaskic. In the meantime I checked, and I informed the Prosecution that it seems it is not -- it was not. However, I am sure that I got this document much earlier during the first phase of my investigation and, in addition to that, the document was discovered in those recent discoveries in Zagreb. But I had it much, much earlier. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the little schedule that has just been handed in can be added to in this way, I think. The first entry, D80/2, is identical with Z516.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That being an exhibit which has been produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as for the cross-examination of this witness as the Chamber will, of course, be aware, depending on whether Mr. Cerkez gives evidence himself or not, this may effectively be his case, this and perhaps the following witness. Mindful of the overall time constraints, it simply won't be possible for me to explore everything with this witness or anything like, and I shan't even attempt to do so. I shall, accordingly, explore some topics with him. I will review the position at the break in order to thereafter give you and Mr. Kovacic a timetable forecast, but I hope I will be excused for leaving for argument things that it simply won't be possible in time to cover in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You won't be criticised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major Sajevic, just a couple of things because they are not clear to me. You lived and live in Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your -- it's not entirely clear to me what your job was, your role in 1992 and 1993. How do you describe yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of 1992, I still worked at the Territorial Defence headquarters. I think that in May 1992, I transferred to the municipal staff of the HVO. Actually, we all did almost everything there. The work that was there was more or less evenly distributed amongst us. There weren't any clear-cut assignments and appointments because it's not a military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first have a clearly-defined military task in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What is a military task? In my opinion, a military task is everything that we did as well in order to prepare those groups that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you have a clear military job title first in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not have any military title in the municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first have a clearly-defined title and a clearly-defined job?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I had a clearly-defined title and clearly-defined job was in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, that is to say, the end of 1992 in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your job then was as?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked in the operations department as an operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your next job title or your next military job was what?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My next military title was within the command of the Viteska Brigade, and I was chief of operations of the operations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cerkez's deputy, effectively?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, according to military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that, as it were, there's nobody between you and Cerkez who would have a better view or should have a better view of what Cerkez was doing at the material times; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's hard to tell because Mr. Cerkez, as commander of the brigade, had several assistants who were in charge of various divisions, so I as head of the operations department --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. We want to know who is the person next down from Cerkez who can give the clearest picture of what he was doing on a day-to-day basis and what he was doing at the time of Ahmici. If it wasn't you, tell us who is the person to whom we should turn for the best information?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think those were all the assistant commanders who, according to the establishment of the brigade, worked on these jobs. They all had the same rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many of them were there and what were their names, quite quickly, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I don't know how fast I can explain all of this. I would have to explain the entire structure of the command of the Viteska Brigade or any other brigade for that matter; also its establishment and various positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. It will seem that I'm racing you, but there are real problems with time in these courts and therefore, if you can help with precise answers to precise questions, it will help us. How many assistant commanders, what were their names?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do them one at a time. There was the chief of the operations department, the assistant commander for logistics; then there was assistant commander for security affairs, for intelligence affairs; then within the operations department there were the officers in charge of engineering, signals; again, within logistics, there were officers in charge of quartermaster services, the ambulance, the medical unit, et cetera. So that would be the main part of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A pretty well-formed brigade, in reality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in reality, it was far from a pretty well-formed brigade, in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look, please, at one entry on our Exhibit 353. It relates to the previous witness. It's got a tag on it. If you'd lay it on the ELMO so that we could see that entry, or some of it. Sorry, wrong Exhibit number. This is 2332.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can see there the name Slavko Jukic and you can see that name there yourself. When we look to the right-hand side of what's displayed on the ELMO overhead projector, we can see that he is registered as having started on the 10th of April of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe that that is correct, because these lists that you are presenting, as far as I can see, were drawn up after the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the years of service of these persons would be registered, so to speak, so that all the soldiers who took part in the war would regulate their status in the best possible way. Did you say this was April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in front of you, if you'd like to look at it.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. 1994? Well, possibly these were the beginnings -- I don't know. I don't remember that some kind of actions had started at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My suggestion to you, or my question to you is this: The entry beside this man's name does not fit with an account of his registering first for work with the HVO on the 16th of April of 1993, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The entry for April 1992, which is a document of your organisation, doesn't fit with, is not consistent with, the suggestion that this person first registered with the HVO on the 16th of April of 1993, does it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know when this person first registered in the HVO. If it was the 10th of April, 1992, I'm not aware of that, because at that time I was not in the municipal staff and at the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Any other document that you can point us to which would give accurate start dates for people's engagement with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot provide any such document, because there was not a single date when it was said: Well, from this date onwards, everybody was in the HVO. People reported spontaneously to -- I don't know -- their friends, in their villages, in their hamlets; in that sense, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't really an establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the date in this column is the date when they are recorded as first registering; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well. It's not very well focused. Can I have a look at the document itself, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the dates. Those are the dates. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I turn to blocks of topics and indeed chronological events, I want to ask you a couple of questions about yourself. After Ahmici, your position of authority in relation to the various detention facilities in Vitez was such that you were the person who released a man called Zlotrg. Do you remember that? You drove him home, I think.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My authority certainly did not include anybody's release. I think it was agreed when the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Red Cross came to visit. According to some kind of plan, this was worked out. And it is true that I drove Mr. Nedim Zlotrg to his apartment, but that was late in the evening, so the release stopped. This evolved in a regular fashion. He was the last person to be released that evening, and it continued on a regular basis the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why did he have to sign a document saying that he had not been tortured, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of him having signed that kind of a document, or anybody else, for that matter. I did not give them such documents to sign. Truth to tell, that evening I did work on registering their release; however, already the next day I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next couple of questions, with the Court's leave, can they be dealt with in private session for witness protection? It will only be a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, this Court is concerned to find out who was responsible for acts that may be shown to be criminal in Vitez in the time you were there as deputy to Cerkez. Now, will you please tell us who was in charge of the detention facilities including the Vitez cinema in 1993? Who had responsibility for what was done there? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for detention facilities and the headquarters, it was the military police, the 4th Battalion of the Military Police that was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Where's this documented, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where this is documented, but that was the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have said -- in fact, that it was in a private session. For this purpose, the previous answer, Your Honour, I propose to mention because it doesn't touch on the matter for which we were in private session. Your immediate previous answer, Major, when I asked you a similar question was that, "If I was referring to the person who was in charge, it was the commander of the brigade." Now, now that you've had explained to you the significance of the person who was in charge of the detention facilities, are you changing your evidence? Are you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not change it. If you remember, we explained it yesterday well or rather I explained it well that until August -- and there is a document -- until August, I don't remember the exact date, the commander of the brigade was not in charge of the military policemen who were there, and it was only in August that Mr. Blaskic ordered the part of the military police which was at the headquarters to place itself under the command of the brigade commander. That was sometime in August. I don't remember the exact date. And that document exists; I saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to return to the military police as a separate topic later in the questions I'm going to ask of you, Major. That's a rather different question from the question I've asked you. As to detention facilities throughout Vitez, and there were several of them, is it your case that the brigade commander had nothing to do with it or is it your case that the brigade commander for Vitez, Cerkez, was in charge?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, there were no detention facilities in Vitez or prisons or facilities specifically organised for the purpose. There were departments where able-bodied of Bosniak ethnicity were brought in the early days of the war. It was in that Workers' University cinema, it is a cinema, and so on and so forth, but those were not detention facilities. That is number one. And, sorry, I forgot your second question in this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question to you was: Is it your case, is it your evidence that the brigade commander had nothing to do with the detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had to do with those facilities in the sense that the headquarters of the brigade were in that particular facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may have to return --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you mean -- you call them "detention facilities" and I affirm they did not exist. The brigade commander had nothing to do with them; yes, that is what I affirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may have to return to that later. Let's turn to Ahmici, shall we? Now you, of course, were unfortunately sick on the night itself. Certain questions follow from that, but can you help me first, please, with an approximate timetable of your presence at brigade headquarters, just giving us the times of the night and the following morning when you went there, because I haven't managed to isolate what time you did first go on the evening of the 15th to the headquarters, roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening of the 15th, in the command, that is after the second time phone call, I arrived somewhere between 2000 and 2100 or perhaps half past 8.00. I can't really tell you a minute by the time I got dressed and got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine. How long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I stayed more than 45 minutes to about one hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your next visit?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time I came, the next morning around half past 5.00, perhaps quarter past 5.00. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long did you stay?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly. I know it was past 7.00, that is, other people had already arrived and I went to see the doctor. Whether that was half past 7.00 or 8.00 or half past 8.00, I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is the period of time covering half past 5.00, 6.00, 6.30 when you are telling us absolutely nothing unusual was reported; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, from somewhere on the ground, people reported that one could hear a fire shot here and there roughly in the northeastern part of the municipality, that is, in the direction of Ahmici, Kuber, and so on and so forth. But no concrete reports came in as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then after having gone to the doctor, your next visit to the brigade headquarters was when?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next time I came, the next day in the morning again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 17th and at what time?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think around 7.00, half past, because I first went to be given the injection and then I reported to the command, spent there a short while and then went back home again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, because of your ill health, you are unable to give us a full account or any account firsthand of what Cerkez was doing. Will you now please tell us who, on his staff, would be able to tell us what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But since I wasn't there all the time, I naturally cannot know which one of my colleagues was in the command all the time. I presume there were certain jobs which took them elsewhere so I cannot really say that so and so spent the whole time in the command, because he may have gone after some business or other somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, you have been allowed by the rules of this Tribunal to give your opinion on troop dispositions on whether Cerkez did things or didn't do things. You were Cerkez's deputy. You know how the army works. Now, please tell us so that we can go and speak to them. Who, on that night, will know what Cerkez was doing?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, that should have been the duty officer of the brigade, and he should have known where the commander was or what he was doing, because when a commander leaves the command, he does not tell everybody where he is going. He tells the person who is on duty that he is going either to have a rest or home or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty officer on the 15th, it was Josip Zuljevic, because he was the one who called me on the telephone at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a person that's going to be at base. Who would have been out with Cerkez on manoeuvres or whatever he was doing that night? You know the way he worked. You tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was out with Cerkez or where Cerkez was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you not give us any idea of who we should turn to, who we should look to for a firsthand account of what Cerkez was doing on that night? Is that what you're really telling us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that I am saying, I am saying as it really was. And the only man who, in my view, or at least that is how it should be, who should have known where Mr. Cerkez was or what he was doing was the brigade duty officer. He is the one who needs to have this information because it can also happen that the superior command needs the commander and then they call the duty officer and ask him. They do not ask for anyone else; they ask for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Josip Zuljevic, where does he live these days if he's still alive?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is alive, and he lives in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, a village near Vitez, a couple of kilometres, not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that after Ahmici happened, you were able to construct what had happened by speaking to the limited number of people who had been engaged who were willing to talk. Your terms were, "The few who were willing to talk." So can we have the names of those people, please, the few people who were involved in Ahmici and the attacks on the other villages who were willing to talk?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of these stories, and there were many of them, I wasn't able to reconstruct the events, but I did talk to quite a number of people because people talked between themselves about what had happened, not the direct participants. I do not know any single participant, direct participant in the Ahmici events. I can tell approximately, but I cannot really point my finger and say this man was in Ahmici. And the first information that I received that something had happened in Ahmici, I was told that by a driver who, a couple of days later, was taking me to the front line and we were talking in the car, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'll look up the quotation over the break and bring it back to your attention, but unless my recollection is wrong, you spoke of contacts with and information from a few people who were present who were willing to talk. I must suggest to you, Major, it is inconceivable, in your position, that you do not know, A, who was involved; and B, that when you said you got information from the few who were willing to talk, you weren't identifying people who had provided an account of what had happened. So let's break that down into two parts. Name us, please, the people who you know to have been involved in the Ahmici crimes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim under full responsibility that I do not know a single name, that is, the name of a man who directly participated in the crime in Ahmici, not a single one. I do not know a single name. And what you are saying now, that I must have known about it, I wouldn't agree with that, because simply the brigade, or rather that part which we called the Vitez Brigade, the Viteska Brigade, had other tasks. We were holding the front line against the Serb aggressor. And after all, the brigade command had its hands full organising the brigade. I claim again, under full responsibility, I do not know the name of a single man who directly participated in Ahmici, and that is how it is. And the stories were circulated later. The whole town talked about it. Women partaking of coffee talked about this. But they are all talks and rumours, and I also -- and guesses and conjectures. I also heard that. People who did not want to talk about this -- well, I presume that direct participants did not want to talk about that, and that is why we do not know them. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If it's in answer to my question, of course.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, as I was saying, later on, hearing those stories, I heard that it was Jokers who took part in Ahmici. But from the outset, that unit -- and I never knew that they had their unit systematisation book or anything. To me they were just a group of people. So I heard that they were in Ahmici alongside parts of the 4th Battalion of the military police. This grouping, to call it that -- the Jokers, I mean -- was, as far as I know, composed not only of men from Vitez but from all parts of the Lasva Valley, so that I did not really have to know the names of all those people, nor did we, as a brigade, have any points of contact with them. So I really -- why should I know who those men were? True, I knew two men from Vitez who were members of Jokers. I had known them from before and I knew that they were with Jokers. But what they were doing, where they were, I didn't -- I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just go back to the first visit at 8.00 on the evening of the 15th. Who was there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the brigade duty officer -- I'm sure about him -- Josip Zuljevic. Then whether at that same time, or perhaps he arrived five or ten minutes later, the commander, Mario Cerkez. There was also Srecko Petrovic, I think. He was, well, say, the cook for the command. They had a small kitchen there. And there were other members of the command, but I cannot really say who was there exactly, because I don't recall. The command wasn't a large one, so I cannot really say exactly. We met every day, and on that day, on that specific day, to remember who was there and who wasn't, I really can't remember. But there was somebody else who was on the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was an important meeting. You had been dragged in off your sick bed. Apart from a cook and Cerkez, who else with any command over any of the groups that were operating in Vitez was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that I attended the meeting. I said that I had come to the command and asked the duty officer first why all the urgencies, as he could see that I was ill. I then asked the commander, "So what's it all about?" and the commander explained it to me that they were expecting certain activities from the direction -- not as if they were expecting, but that he had received information from the military district that they were expecting the ABiH activities from the direction of Kruscica and Vranjska and that we should reinforce or, rather, deploy a couple of men if they started downhill to prevent them entering the town. And then he told me to look at the operative documents, and I said, "Well, can it be done in the morning, because I can barely stand on my feet?" And he said, "Right. Yes, of course you can. Get back to bed," because he would see that I was all in sweat and I could barely stand. And whether there was a meeting after that, I don't know, because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your position within the brigade, and in your position in Vitez, if there was a coordinated attack on the morning of the 16th of April on a number of villages, with those attacking being supported by artillery and perhaps protected from intervention by UNPROFOR, to which I'll return, somebody had to coordinate the attack. On whose shoulders did coordination in Vitez fall, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the attack which took place on the 16th of April, in the morning, then you have to look for that coordinator amongst the ranks of the BH army, because they were the attackers; that is, they must have had within their ranks and in their command somebody who coordinated that attack, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, who then -- who coordinated the defence, if you say it was a defence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the Vitez Brigade, the defence was coordinated by Mr. Cerkez, in that part of the front, that is, in that area which had been assigned to us through the orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And your case, or your evidence, is that then the Jokers and the 4th Battalion of the military police went off and committed the massacre in Ahmici; is that what you say, you would ask us believe to have happened?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say it with certainty, but from all these stories, from all the information that one could obtain immediately afterwards in the wake of it, and then later on throughout the conflict, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, who had the artillery to go on Mosunj hill or feature and fire the first shot that indicated the attack was to take place, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that the first shot was fired from Mosunj and that it signalled the beginning of the attack, because Mosunj is an exclusively Croat village, which means that I do not really believe that anyone could have given any sign, if you mean a sign for the beginning of combat operations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How could the Jokers or the military police have had artillery support, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that they had any artillery support, nor how they could get it. How they could get it, it was through the military district, because the military district included also the artillery infantry unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Cerkez's responsibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Then whose artillery would be supporting, please? Whose artillery would be supporting the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I do not know that anyone's artillery lent support. And if there was any support, I do not know about it. But if there was any support, then in no case the Vitez Brigade could do that, because the Vitez Brigade did not have its artillery, never, until the end of the war; never, ever. In the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia there was the Mixed Artillery Rocket Regiment, which was under the direct command of the Operative Zone command, and throughout Central Bosnia no commander could have that formation under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. So that's Blaskic, is it? Blaskic is responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that Blaskic was responsible for it, but Blaskic was the commander-in-chief. And yes, he could command that artillery battalion. But he also had his chief of artillery, and he was, of course, the first disappearer of that battalion, of that formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On your account, as you summarised it in answer to His Honour, the military police and the Jokers committed these atrocities. Who directed them? Who coordinated their activities, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that it was through stories which have circulated for days. But I think that they were true, and that is how I learnt about the whole thing. But who was the Jokers' commander at that time, I don't know. And I believe that the commander of the military police was Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the coordination would have to come from what? Blaskic? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how many times I have to repeat this. The Vitez Brigade had no points of contact with the Jokers, and with the military police only insofar as several military policemen provided security for our command. And that was all. So I did -- I was not concerned with those two units, nor could I or anyone else have any influence on their work, nor did I know who coordinated their work. They must have had within their ranks one man or perhaps a couple of men. I don't really know what principles they were governed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Kordic have a line of authority, to your knowledge, to the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of something like that at all, and I don't see how, because Mr. Kordic was a politician. He wasn't a military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought you didn't know who commanded the Jokers. How can you say that Mr. Kordic didn't if you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I think that Mr. Kordic didn't, does not, couldn't have command in any way or have any influence on the Jokers, on the command, because he was not a military man; he was not an officer. That is what I meant. And it is true that I do not know who was the Jokers' commander at that time. I really don't. I don't to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you don't know, but your evidence is that it must have been a military person; is that what you're saying, that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was a military person, because it was sort of an army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. I should like to understand what the witness is saying. In his answer to the President, he said that the Jokers and the military police were the ones who perpetrated the massacre. But could you tell us, when these coordinated activities happened on the 16th of April, could you tell us: Could they have intervened in a part of the territory which was covered by the Vitez Brigade, which was under the Vitez Brigade? Because there was a certain territory -- this brigade was covering certain territory, certain area, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. The brigade did cover a certain area; that is, the brigade was formed in the territory of the municipality of Vitez. And in a manner of speaking, it was to control the territory of the Vitez municipality, which was under the control of Croats, to put it that way, because a large part of the municipality was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, there was something else there, and that is the existence of the military district at headquarters in Vitez itself, and that was the superior command to the Vitez Brigade and all the other brigades in Central Bosnia. This is one thing. Secondly, the Vitez Brigade -- and I repeated it repeatedly, several times -- was never organised in line with documents which envisaged the formation of brigades. That is, it was never fully -- it never existed in full strength and with all the materiel, with all the armament, not to mention its organisation and the whole system. So according to some army rules, and I believe they can be likened to the rules that exist in armies in other countries, a brigade cannot cover that size of the territory of that length of the front line. There is no brigade in the world which could cover a front line 52 kilometres long. Not even a division can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but you did not answer my question. The events which happened on the 16th of April that we are talking about, in a village, and I'm referring to the massacre in Ahmici, did these things happen in an area which was under the responsibility, even if formal, even if theoretical, which was under the full responsibility of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically, yes, but across the municipality of Vitez -- and I should say that the same thing happened in Busovaca, in Travnik -- these, if I may call them so, these autonomous -- these groups, these special purpose units, as they called them, could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're answering to me yes, that in effect, yes, these things happened in a part of the territory which was normally under the control of the Vitez Brigade. Now, how is it possible that this brigade did not respond to an event which was happening nearby? Because, after all, it was only a few kilometres away, so why wasn't there any reaction? You tell us that the Vitez Brigade did not react at all. Can one imagine that it would not react at all at a time when it would be normally responsible for that part of the territory? You know that the commander, who had some territorial responsibility, that he should know what is going on around him.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to show, with the help of maps, the positions of the BH army forces or, rather, the territory which was under their control. The Vitez Brigade could not control Ahmici because not a single member of the Vitez Brigade or a Croat was in that part. Those were men from some units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was that. You asked me how is it that the brigade did not react to the events in Ahmici. Well, it did not react simply because we were not aware of what was happening, at least I didn't. For a couple of days we simply did not know what had happened. Secondly, all those units which did not make part of the Vitez Brigade, they freely moved around the area. They were not under a command so we did not know where those units were at every given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that in point of fact the Vitez Brigade had no authority over the territory which was part of the territory of the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, evidently, if one refers to the whole territory, the Vitez Brigade was receiving its orders from the military district, full parts of the front line which were held by men of the Vitez Brigade and that was that area of responsibility, because in some cases later on in the course of the war, there were such instances when we needed assistance from other brigades. Then, at the level of the military district, that is the Operative Zone, certain segments of the positions would be assigned which were then helped, whether we were helped out by members of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, Zrinjski, and so on. And for a certain period of time when the offensive was slackened, they would go back to their own units so that was that. If the responsibility of the brigade amounted only to what had been assigned to it by an order and the brigade, that is, that part which we keep calling brigade because in no case can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But your orders came from whom? From whom did these orders come?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were receiving our orders from the military district, that is, from the superior command, the immediate superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who exactly?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander. It was Commander Tihomir Blaskic who was the commander of the military district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Following Their Honour's questions, just these two supplementary ones before we turn to look at some documents. If what you are telling us is true, and that there was a perceived threat in the Vitez area, then there should have been a coordinated defence involving the Viteska Brigade, the Jokers, if they were available, the military police and so on. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not correct. First of all, because the Jokers and the military police were never under the command of the Vitez Brigade, that is what I keep saying. And secondly, you are right in as far as if there was information that an overall attack was imminent, of course defence would be organised, that would be normal. But it would be normal for a true defence to be organised with the real units, who would be trained, well-equipped, fully-manned, and we had none of that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. As I said yesterday, the 300 men who were listed as members of the Vitez Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... because I want you to be responsive to the questions I ask. I was asking you in general terms not whether there would be coordination by the Viteska Brigade but whether there would be a coordinated defence. And I think your answer to the question is: If there was information of risk of the type I summarised, suggested, there would be a coordinated defence coordinated, perhaps, by Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably at the level of the superior command, they would evaluate the situation and probably at that level, they would coordinate the work of the Vitez Brigade, the Zrinjski Brigade, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. I assume that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You, with all your contemporaneous knowledge, and I'll just tell you what it was you actually said to us yesterday, what you said was, "Needless to say," -- this is page 77 of the way it's formulated yesterday, line 14. You said this, "Needless to say, I have been receiving more and more information about this to this day. Few people were willing to talk about it, at least of those who participated in that so far as I know." And you then went on to say something about the specific reports or something in writing, "I never had in my hands. So basically I do not know what happened there and how it happened." Now, I come back to my question. With the information you've received, you've been able to tell the Judges, quite emphatically, that Cerkez and the Viteska Brigade had nothing to do with it so you've obviously got a lot of detail. Are you really suggesting that at the same time as the Viteska Brigade was ordered to conduct a legitimate defence, other units were being coordinated to go and conduct an entirely criminal attack? Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that the Vitez Brigade, at the time in question, had a clear and specific order from the superior command as to where and how they should position some of their men, and the Vitez Brigade did this. I also assert that the Vitez Brigade did not receive any order nor did it take any action in the area where the village of Ahmici is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can assist the Court in due course with specific order because we are going to have to look at that if that's a matter of concern. It's only a couple of questions away. I want to look at the orders with this witness, in general terms, before I refocus on the specific order that he's dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness is talking about a very precise order to take positions in certain places, that is, could we have this -- what kind of a decision was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've heard the learned Judge, Major. What kind of decision, what kind of order was it that, as you understand it, Cerkez and the Viteska Brigade received?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an order, the order that was here on the table yesterday, that parts of the Vitez Brigade should take up positions facing Vranjska and Kruscica and, if necessary, to prevent the passage of forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Kruscica in the direction of town. As far as I can remember, that is what the order says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As far as your direct evidence is concerned, what you can tell us directly was that you were ill at the headquarters the night before for a short period, you spoke to Mr. Cerkez and heard certain things from him. The next day, sometime before 7.00, again, ill, you returned to the headquarters for a short time. You never saw where the brigade was. You were merely told things. You can't give direct evidence as to what happened at Ahmici. You've had conversations with people from which you formed various views yourself or you were told various things. Those conversations suggested that various units were the perpetrators, but no individuals were mentioned. Is that a fair description of what you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we look at the documents then, just one more question for you, as a military man, as you were. It would be utter folly for a military commander to instruct units under his command to be doing mutually contradictory things, one unit ignorant of what the other was doing; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your question? I did not fully understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask it perhaps in another way. It would be folly to have units under your command, if you are a commanding officer, ignorant of what each other was doing. You've got one unit massacring Ahmici, and another unit in an adjacent area acting in defence. It would be folly not to keep one informed of what the other was doing.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one unit may or may not know what another unit is doing. It depends on where they are, how far away they are from each other, what their assignments are and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will you, as a military man, please, try to deal with the basic propositions I have put to you, and then you can deal with it specifically relating to Blaskic and these events. General principle, if you've got people working on the same territory or an immediately adjacent territory, under your command, you keep one informed of what the other is doing, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If you mean to say -- I don't understand you fully. Are you saying that one brigade should inform another brigade of its activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just deal with it specifically and then this really will be the last question on this topic. From all that you've learned, can you give any sensible reason why Blaskic should have instructed the military police and the Jokers to have carried out the attacks on Ahmici and other villages and yet to have kept Viteska in the dark? Can you give any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that one fact was implied. I would not like to warn the witness, but one fact which was implied which was never said here, not particularly by this witness, he is not able to understand that. That question should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you objecting to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference to Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, without a reference to Blaskic, perhaps you could rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you think of any reason, please, whether it was Blaskic, Kordic or anyone masterminding the events on the 15th and 16th should have instructed the Jokers and the military police to go and attack certain villages while keeping the Viteska Brigade completely in the dark about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether these were the instructions, the orders. Whether Blaskic issued them or not, I am not qualified to say, because I don't know. I don't know how this happened. But why Mr. Blaskic did not inform the Vitez Brigade, he probably did not think it necessary. He does not have to inform every brigade if he issues an order to another unit. He doesn't have to explain his orders or expand upon them so I don't know the reason why he did not inform them. He probably did not think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we now look, and I can save time by probably handing my copies in straight away, at the original of 660, and -- because I want to look at the document, if it can go straight on the ELMO, the original of 660.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 660 being a reference to the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order, focus on date, please, at the top. This is an order of the 15th of April of 1993. I'm so sorry, can I have it back? I've just noticed something that I haven't noticed before. It is my mistake. Right. Well, I better deal with it in this way if you put the English version on to begin with and I better explain something to the Chamber that I was going to explain in any event in relation to another document. Your Honour, these orders from Blaskic, many of them were first produced in the Blaskic trial. When they were first produced by counsel for Blaskic, the numbers had been x-ed out and the document had been recopied so the number didn't appear for whatever reason. In respect of some documents, the numbers were subsequently retrieved so that in this case, we can see that the document from another version has been discovered as having the number 01-4-227 of 1993. In fact, if you look at the original, this is obviously the generation that came in the Blaskic trial, because if the usher would be good enough to show us the original, we can see the number isn't there although the space for the number is. None of this concerns the Major, and I'm sorry not to have, in fact, realised this and got whatever document exists to support the number. I'll try and find it. But if I can ask the Major this question, looking now at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, you don't have to trouble with much of what I have just said to the learned Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He hasn't put the question yet, so you can't object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will not object on the question. I am objecting to the document because it seems that we are talking about two different documents according to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the documents are wrongly associated, I am very sorry, and, again, that will have to be tidied up. But it would appear, Major, we can satisfy everyone of this in due course, that on the 15th of April of 1993, if you look at the English version, this much should be easily understood, that there was an order from Blaskic at 1545 hours and its number was 227/93. You received orders from Blaskic. That's the way he did things; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's logical for us to receive orders from the superior commander. That's the military hierarchy. That's the chain of command. That's how it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The important point is he numbered his documents. He had serial numbers, in this case, number 227 of 1993 for his documents or 227 for the month of April. I don't know how it operated. And if you'd now like to please look at -- in this case it does work, the original of 681 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't think you've got a specific answer to that question, but he numbered the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to show him the next one and I think we'll see the point, I hope. 681, and the original will serve the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a Blaskic order, as we can see, at 9.15 on the morning of the 16th of April, and we see the serial number now is 278. So assuming that the serial numbers are used in an ordinary and obvious way, some 50 documents were generated by Blaskic in the intervening period of time. So my question to you as a man who received, amongst other documents, these orders is this: Blaskic used serial numbers for his documents in a sequential way as suggested by these two documents; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, with all due respect, sir, I think you are mistaken. I'll tell you why. The numbers that are put on documents are the numbers in the entry book, the register, where all the documents are entered. I do not know exactly what method was used in the Operative Zone, how they entered their documents in the register, because every brigade had its own method of recording documents. And what could have happened was that orders would have a certain number -- an order would have a certain kind of number, an instruction would have another kind of number, another kind of document would have a third kind of number. So in my opinion, it does not point to a sequence of documents. These are not ordinal numbers which would show that between these two documents 50 other documents had been issued. Simply this, as you see, is entitled "Protest," so it's possible that it might have been entered in another sequence. So all the documents issued sequentially from the Operative Zone do not necessarily have ordinal numbers in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can entirely accept there may be more than one sequence, and just, since you raise that point, I may be able to meet it, if the Chamber will just indulge me for a minute. In fact, I don't think I can, at the moment, in any event. But I'd like you now, please, to look at the document that you concerned with yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's, in fact, 11.00. Would this be a convenient moment, or do you want to ask about that particular document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the break is as convenient as now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have now located a version of Z660, which doesn't have the number snowpacked out of it, and I'll make that available to everyone in due course. Before I move on, the actions of accounts in the Blaskic case in wiping the numbers out means that we've got to be cautious before inferring anything from those generated documents where numbers aren't there. With that in mind, can the witness now, please, look at Exhibit 683.1, produced yesterday as D60/2, 683.1, which is indeed a document which has had the number erased in the original. And it's the document I think Judge Bennouna had in mind this morning in asking questions about instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, Major, you looked at this document yesterday, and I want to know a few things from you, please. When are you saying you first saw this document?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, I can't say for sure. Quite a bit of time had passed until I saw it. I did not see it during that first time. I can't say exactly when I first saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did you see it simply by chance, or did you see it in the course of considering the events of the night of the 15th, 16th, or what? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I cannot say exactly when I first saw this document. I think I first saw it when the archives were being sorted, this documentation. Simply when -- when at one moment -- well, perhaps this was the end of 1993, when the archives of our brigade were being sorted, compiled, in order to have documents compiled in one place, because documents were wandering about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you saw it, you didn't associate it particularly with any other document prepared and sent the same night, or did you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all these documents that came in during that night, I actually saw only later. As far as the contents of this document are concerned, I found out about this from Mr. Cerkez. He told me about it. So I didn't think it was necessary in that chaos and all that to ask for that document, to see that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez what, told you about it? Well, when did he tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 15th, in the evening. He said that it would arrive. When I asked whether there was a written order for all the activities that the brigade was supposed to carry out, or rather to take this area as ordered, he said that the written order had not arrived yet but that it was supposed to arrive during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this, so that we can understand it, if it was on the 15th, it has to be in that 45 minutes between 8.00 and 8.30; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I think it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you saying, so that I can follow this, are you saying that all of what we find set out here on this document -- and please have another look at it -- all of what we find here was already forecast by Cerkez to you in that meeting on the evening of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that he said all of this to me verbatim, but he gave me the essence. I can't remember now. I mean, you know, he didn't have the document in front of himself. He wasn't reading from it, but he conveyed the essence of this document to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell me: There was discussion of a possible Muslim attack, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What intelligence had you had about a Muslim attack?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that we had some special intelligence. Intelligence was mainly channelled to the headquarters [as interpreted], and whatever the command headquarters thought that we should know that pertained to our brigade, that is what they sent to us. As for this intelligence, well, the entire intelligence situation was being monitored all the time, in view of the incidents that had occurred. There were some indications that some sabotage groups were being prepared that could possibly be sent into the territory of Vitez -- sabotage, diversion groups -- and this information was heard even before the 15th, but I cannot assess how correct this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, may I intervene? The witness said -- "the intelligence which was channelled to the headquarters": That is in the record. The witness said "to the higher, superior headquarters." The word "superior" or "higher" headquarters is missing, and that is changing the thing substantially. We need that word. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, what we can be sure of is this: At the very least, the records of Blaskic will contain, or should contain, a document or documents showing what attack was feared that led to these actions on the night of the 15th, 16th.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know now about the quality of the intelligence itself, whether they were corroborated by some documents. In the military, the intelligence service does not have to write a document accompanying every piece of information. That is one thing. Secondly, every information can be either 100 per cent sure, well-founded; then it cannot be thoroughly checked out; and then there can be others that are yet to be checked out. But information is information. I'm sorry. I don't know that there is a document that would present the actual intelligence situation on the ground to Mr. Blaskic. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There also ought to be a record, written record, of Blaskic's explanation of the risk to your Commander Cerkez, shouldn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what kind of risk are you referring to, risk from an attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the risk from an attack should have been in a document sent to Cerkez by Blaskic. We can see how meticulous Blaskic was with his letter writing and his order giving.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every order to a subordinate unit concerning combat operations, it is necessary to have what is objectively possible and also the information available about the enemy at that time. That is the methodology according to which orders are worked out. So he probably gave, through all the orders, what he deemed necessary to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see there are two possibilities I'm going to ask you to consider, possibly three, but certainly two. One is that there was intelligence about information about a possible attack and it was genuine, that is it was genuine information. The other alternative is that although an attack may have been talked about or a threatened attack may have been talked about -- that although a threatened attack may have been talked about, it was entirely fabricated and it was mentioned simply as an excuse for what was to happen on the morning of the 16th. Now those are two possibilities. Can you help us by any document to show that the discussion of a threatened attack by the BiH was genuine as opposed to something simply being made up to justify what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why that would be an excuse. That's not clear to me. I cannot show you any document about an attack of the BH army being expected 100 per cent for sure. Very often, during the war, there has to be an overall assessment of the situation on the ground where all factors are considered that could bring about a worsening of the situation and possibly lead to a conflict. So this assessment, on the basis of which General Blaskic probably issued such orders, is based upon something -- on some kind of information that he had. That, I don't know. However, through this specific order, one can also see that we should just be ready if there is a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, still in keeping with this decision that I had asked a question about, it was said necessary to have a look at it to have an idea of the type of orders that were delivered on that day of the 16th of April. Could the witness tell us how he understands paragraph two. I read in English. [In English] "The assignment of your forces is to occupy the defence region, the blockade of villages, and prevent all entrances to and exits from the villages." [Interpretation] Therefore, paragraph two, apparently deals with the defence of the region. It mentions villages in general whilst the first paragraph is more specific as to the direction to be taken. Paragraph two mentions the defence region, the blockade of villages, and the fact of preventing all entrances to and exits from the villages. Could the witness tell us what the region is that he is speaking about, the region which is supposed to be defended?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific region can be seen in paragraph one of this order, that is the area that gravitates towards the villages of Kruscica and Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when they mention villages in general, what are the villages mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two villages that are mentioned in paragraph one. When it says "villages," it is the plural, and it is those two villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you are of the view that paragraph two does not deal with the specific territory that would be under the command of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that paragraph two does deal with a specific territory, a specific part of the municipality where the Viteska Brigade has the task of locating that part towards these two villages. That's specific for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But, Major, you haven't even begun to address the letter as whole, look at the heading, "Blockade the broader territory of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska." It's not the two villages to start with, is it, nothing like?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. I just paid attention to paragraph one, that's true, the preamble says Donja Veceriska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And before we put the map on the ELMO, just look at the last sentence, please, of paragraph one. "The enemy will probably use infantry units, but will direct G/S at the command headquarters and other HVO institutions." Was your activity really limited to just these two villages?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our activity was limited to these two villages because as far as the village of Donja Veceriska is concerned, as far as the village of Donja Veceriska is concerned, it can be seen from this order that that's where the civilian police forces were, that is to say, that the Viteska Brigade had the exclusive task of dealing with those two villages that are mentioned in paragraph one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you follow the Blaskic trial when it was going on in this place?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain, please, how it was that Blaskic was talking to Cerkez on the morning of the 16th with Cerkez being in Donja Veceriska and seeking assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may intervene. That is merely assertion. That was not mentioned in no document, no testimony, nothing. It is -- the purpose, I doubt, is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness says he doesn't know anything about it. Counsel is entitled to put things. It's a matter of whether the witness accepts them or not but it's not, of course, evidence if counsel puts something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I wanted to find out from the witness the distance between those villages mentioned: Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska on the one hand, and Ahmici on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we lay the map on top of the document, because I will be returning to the document, the map number is 273.2 -- I haven't got the number, but I'll get it right in a minute. This map, Your Honour, contrary to what I said on an earlier occasion, the squares are two-kilometre squares so that if we look a little bit to the left of where we are at the moment or focus down on to Ahmici and Nadioci to the right with Pirici above them, and Santici on the main road, one can see there the distance. And if we run to the left -- if the usher would be so good to move it across a little bit further to the left as well -- we then come to Vitez and we can see the river running up and crossing the road south -- north of Divjak. Then Donja Veceriska lies just south-west of Divjak, and then I think I may seek the witness' -- no, sorry, Kruscica we can see now dead centre and to the bottom of the map marked as an area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where are the other two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can help us with them. We need -- Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can see Vranjska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Vranjska, yes, is indeed an area there, yes. I hope that helps because the scale of the map is shown at the foot of it, and it seems clear that each square is two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would he still try to give a distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've heard the learned Judge's question, Major. Would you please try and give what you understand to be the distance between Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned three villages now and there are three different distances involved. That is to say Donja Veceriska -- Donja Veceriska, just a minute, please. Donja Veceriska is about six and a half kilometres away from Ahmici, Kruscica about five kilometres, and Vranjska about four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we've got the map there and before I part from it, can we go back just a bit to the left, please, and we see Divjak and Veceriska and we remember that the SPS factory, this is right, Major, isn't it, that lies on that road that is between Donja Veceriska and Gacice, correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What are the other names for that factory or the other factories there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It used to be a single factory there, Slobodan Princip Seljo and then they made different companies, Vitezit, Sintevit, and SPS which is also Slobodan Princip Seljo. Then there were three companies, that is to say -- I can't tell you more about this. I never worked in this company so I don't know about its current set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the bridge, there must be a bridge, do you see, to Divjak. There's a bridge there where the road crosses the river or the river crosses the road, I can't remember which. What's that bridge called?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there is no special name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Divjak bridge, the bridge on Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR forces at the time were located to the north-west of Divjak, beyond that bridge, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part -- one part was to the north-east of Divjak, that is to say, before the bridge, and the other part to the north-west, in Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's come back to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, usher. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can come back to the document. And we've looked at paragraphs 1 and 2, because we see the assignment of forces, paragraph 2: to occupy the defence regions, prevent entrances and exits, and so on. Time of readiness, 0530 on the 16th. A very precise time. Was that because you were being told that the threat from the Muslim forces, genuine or false, was expected at a specific time in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of your question, you say that item 2 shows the intent to occupy villages and take certain positions. That is not true. Item 2 shows that parts of the Vitez Brigade forces should take positions in the territory controlled by Croats; in other words, ahead, in front of the villages in Kruscica and Vranjska, and that they should be ready there in case the BH army attempted to break through from Kruscica and Vranjska, or rather than occupy any villages, they cannot occupy their villages. They were in our own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then we come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you like to answer the question now? You didn't answer the question. You were asked about the time, the very precise time. Can you offer any explanation as to that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every combat order indicates the time of readiness, and time of readiness means the last -- the deadline by which the units need to be ready for a possible action, that is, execute the order. And our formations along this direction executed the order by the very fact of taking those positions in our villages facing those two villages, so that by that time they were expected to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just come back to the time shortly. I suggest to you, you know perfectly well that it's important, and I'll come back to that in a minute. If we move down on the document, if the usher could assist us, to the lower paragraphs. That's fine. They're already there. Thank you very much. If we pass over 3 and 4 for the time being, would you look, please, at paragraph 5, Major. Other points of the command conform to earlier specified instructions. Now, you're being brought here to tell us about what happened, so perhaps you'll tell us about the earlier specified instructions.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say much about item 5, because if these are earlier specified instructions, they could have been transmitted to the brigade commander by the Operative Zone commander either orally or by telephone or perhaps in some other way. I mean, what do I know? I don't know what this is about. I don't know what were those earlier specified instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, you see, you've come here to give us the benefit of what you've learnt from talking to Cerkez, talking to everyone else, looking at maps, and you're not going to tell us or you can't tell us what the earlier specified instructions are? I'm going to suggest to you it's that you're not prepared to.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are entitled to your impressions, but I really tell you that I do not know which are those earlier specified instructions. And what were those instructions, whether they were in writing, were they oral, I don't know; I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was an earlier discussion, at which you may well have been present -- I don't know -- of which you're aware, I'm going to suggest to you, where it was agreed to launch an attack at half past 5.00 on various villages, including Ahmici, and that's what's probably referred to here in "earlier specified instructions."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. I did not attend any previous talks or meetings. I don't know what you mean. I explained to you when I came to the command of the 15th, in the evening, and all that day I hadn't been to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that earlier meeting the fate of Ahmici and the other villages, and the villagers of those villages, was sealed, and you know it, Major; so did Cerkez, on the night itself.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I do not know that that is correct, and I am not aware of any previous agreements -- not agreements, I mean meetings at the military district. Well, that's only natural. There was a meeting every day there. But I was not present there and I wasn't present at a meeting that possibly took place which you are mentioning. And I didn't know that allegedly, as you claim, we were planning to attack Ahmici and other villages, and so on and so forth. I do not know of any such agreement, nor did I take part in any such agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If, as you say, there was some information -- let's call it intelligence -- about a threatened attack by the ABiH, there would be nothing to stop you discussing that with UNPROFOR, would there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
