utterances.text: I don't understand. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would there be any reason why, if you had the general concerns about a threatened attack, you shouldn't discuss it, you shouldn't mention it to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would there be any --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I can't answer that question now. I don't -- I don't know in those moments how people thought and what they talked about seven years ago. I don't know whether I would have talked to UNPROFOR if I were in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, there was certainly no need to keep UNPROFOR out of the information, or come to that, no need to keep UNPROFOR out of the area, was there?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no reason, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the witness, see, please, and then I'm going to turn to another topic, D85/2, the map that he produced yesterday. It may be that this map will be easier to use now that we've reminded ourselves of the map on the larger scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The blue marks drawn by you represent, is this correct, the area of activity of the Viteska Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, yes, the area of activity of the Vitez Brigade, but in part also the positions of the military, that is, civilian police, in the western part, or shall I say left part of the map, because blue indicates the positions which were to be taken by Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So even on your drawing of the map, the right-hand extremity of the Viteska's area of interest is very close to Santici and very close to Ahmici and Nadioci?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, relatively, yes, relatively close, because this area was throughout so narrow, so small, so restricted, that there was no room for any manoeuvres on any larger scale. Quite simply, this area was compressed from both sides, from the north and from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the brigade from Vitez had to join up with the brigade from Busovaca, and where did it join? Somewhere in the region of Rovna or Hrasno? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't that one brigade joined another brigade, but the points of contact were indicated, that is, the place where two brigades came into contact, where they were to physically link up. But neither brigade would enter the area of another brigade. But that was I think somewhere at Rovna. It's difficult to say really, because the relief is such there, it is hilly, there are woods, so even the boundaries of villages are not quite clear. You can't really see them on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, the way you've drawn the green line to the north is that it comes down almost -- indeed comes down to the road at Santici, and then a little to the east of that, just south of Ahmici. You know, don't you, that the attack on Ahmici, from all you've heard, was mounted from that road; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the attack on Ahmici came from. And as for this drawing on the map, we need to understand one thing. When you use such a thick marker on the panel, you cannot really be very precise, because the panel will show a cover of a map, so it cannot be to a metre really precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just, to correct the map, then, because we know that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bungalow of the Jokers was on, I think, the north side of that red road, close to Ahmici and Nadioci. Can we take it that that green line should really be regarded as some distance, at any event, some distance north of that red road, exposing Ahmici and Nadioci to the attack that was made on it from the road?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't understand what you are asking me. This green line that I drew is an imagined line which simply separates the territory which is under the -- how to put it? -- the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, parts of the municipality inhabited by the Bosniak population and where the control was in the hands of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is this imagined line which I marked in green. And nobody can say --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let's worry no more about it, because you can help me with this. If what you're telling us is true and this operation was, so far as the Viteska Brigade was concerned, a legitimate defence operation, there will no doubt be contemporaneous documents, possibly including maps, showing where your troops were disposed and recording what they did; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat this, or at least split it into two questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll break it down and make it as simple as I can. Where are the documents prepared at the time showing the disposition of your troops and recording what they did?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents dating to that time can show only the positions of parts of the Vitez Brigade on the defence line towards Goles, that is, at Slatka Voda and so on. As to this situation here, no combat documents were drawn up. Quite simply, this was a normal situation, to pay so much more attention to a certain part of the municipality, to perhaps send more men there. But there were no special combat documents, nor was there any -- was there adequate, professionally-trained personnel to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, if the document that we've been looking at for half past 1.00 in the morning for the 16th of April is a genuine document in the sense that it was prepared at the time and reflected what orders were given to the Viteska Brigade, would you accept, Major, that there must be documents in existence going from Blaskic to the other parts of the evening's activities, to the Jokers and to the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess -- what do I know? I don't know whether Mr. Blaskic sent any other orders to anyone else or any other documents. How can I know such a thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have been at pains to say things about the military police for the brigade. I'm not sure I understood your evidence yesterday, but does it come to this: You're saying although the term "brigade military police" was used, at the material times there was no such thing as "brigade military police."

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any difference between what happened, so far as you know, what happened to the Viteska Brigade and what happened with other brigades under Blaskic's general command so far as military police was concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke about the military police, I said it yesterday. From the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, parts were sent, I wouldn't call them platoons, but groups of military policemen were sent to other brigades in order to perform those basic functions of the military police. And the same applies to the Viteska Brigade. So that presumably, not presumably but in all likelihood, all those other groups are called brigade military police. But brigade military police not as -- the organic part of the brigade, but simply because, at a given moment, it was with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to other brigades, there is no reason to believe that their relationship with the military police was any different from the relationship that the Viteska Brigade had with the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was in other brigades. I think that it was the same, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You gave a lot of evidence yesterday about the distance, if I can put it in that way, between the military police and the Viteska Brigade. Did you understand that you were giving that evidence because of the importance of there being a distance between the Viteska Brigade and the military police on the night of the 15th, 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you mean. I'm really sorry, but I am simply completely confused as to what you are driving at. Could you simplify your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'll abandon that question and take you through some document swiftly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm afraid these are new documents. They arise from the evidence given yesterday, and I'll try to deal with them quickly. Your Honour, the purpose of this is to try to get the true picture of the military police in Blaskic's area of command before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document, Major, it's not from your brigade, it's from the Gornji Vakuf Brigade. It's dated the 11th of November of 1992 and it's an order that, "Unit commanders are ordered to hold an inspection of their units and describe the existing and spent MTS according to the following schedule," and one of the identified units of that brigade is as of November, 1992, we see third from the bottom, military police. Now, that brigade, if this document is correct, appears to have a military police unit as part of its formation. Can you explain why it should be the case that the Viteska Brigade should be different in some way?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, I cannot properly comment on this document because it has to do with Gornji Vakuf and we were cut off from it even territorially, and I do not know what went on there. But one must bear in mind that the brigade, that is the term "brigade", militarily speaking, does not always denote the same thing. There are different types of brigades. Now, which brigade was formed in Gornji Vakuf, I don't know. There is infantry brigade, there is motorised brigade, mechanised brigade, armoured mechanised brigade, and so on and so forth, and there are all different types of brigades. So I do not know which is this and how was it formed. And in Gornji Vakuf, presumably they had more time and more opportunity to form a brigade, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Next exhibit, 371.1, please. You weren't cut off from Zenica, were you, at the time, or were you in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not cut off from Zenica formally, but I believe there were some checkpoints up at Vjetrenice where the next entrance is from Zenica that were controlled by the members of the BH army. Whether it was their police or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, on the 16th of January, 1993, the command of the Jure Francetic Brigade of Zenica, pursuant to orders received from the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and for replenishing weapons, the order goes out, "Personal weapons distributed to be taken from persons listed below." And then after that it says in paragraph two, "The chief of security and commander of the military police platoon of the Jure Francetic Brigade and the 3rd and 4th platoons of the 4th Military Police Battalion is personally responsible for the implementation of this order." And then it was sent off to the commander of the 3rd and 4th Battalions of the Military Police and to the platoon commander of the Military Police of the Jure Francetic Brigade. So that brigade appeared to have its own military police; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This document doesn't really tell me anything in particular. We cannot see from this document whether the individuals indicated here were members of the Jure Francetic Brigade or were they members of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police and then were attached to that brigade. This document tells me very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Very well. Well, let's look at one for the Travnik Brigade, also the 21st of January, 383.3. This is a document signed by Filip Filipovic and it's to do with salaries. We need only look at the beginning. It's a command of a payment of salaries according to payrolls, and this is what it says under paragraph two, "I am determining those who will effect the pay of salaries in the," presumed to read HVO, it's not very clear, "according to the units as follows: 1st Battle, 2nd Battle, 3rd Battle, Brigade command, and then military police, and then brigade military police." Now, just help us, please. You have come here to tell us all about the military police or a lot about them. Do you accept that the Travnik Brigade had it's own military police?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot accept that the Travnik Brigade had its own police. And as for what it says here, it's quite possible that the person who was supposed to pay out the salaries of these policemen in order to be more efficient and faster, distributed their pay to them. That person probably collected their pay from their command and carried it there because they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to debate it with you but there's already an instruction to the military police separately to Slavica Barovic. This document makes it clear that there are two entirely separate units, there is the military police and there is the brigade military police and you know that, don't you, Major? Because you are trying to mislead the Chamber into thinking there is a greater divide between the military police and between the brigades than, in fact, there was?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of divide you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, for the sake of completeness, I'm not going to show it; it takes time. The Chamber will remember that I put to an earlier witness 545.2, the 16th of March document which was in the form of a request to the HVO Military Police from Cerkez. That was a request not an order. I've already dealt with that. If we look at the next document it's 551.3. It's another request which again, for fullness and fairness, I put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a document, Major, from Cerkez, on the 18th of March requesting people to be brought into custody and being sent to the Vitez Military Police, all right? You'd accept that that's the sort of order that Cerkez would have made, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, according to me, is the regular route to be followed when the military police was used for the purposes of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next exhibit is part of an article from a magazine called Bojovnik which is the HVO's bi-weekly military magazine, correct, or was the HVO's bi-weekly military magazine? Now, I'm just going to read a passage. It's the third sheet in the English version, page six in the B/C/S. This is the article of a soldier who became a military policeman. In the middle of the page in the English version on the third sheet, third page, and I hope you can find this, if necessary, on the sixth sheet goes as follows: "After I left the special unit, I wanted to join the HVO police since there already existed regional HVO police, the commander of which was Dobrica Jonjic who promised to enrol me. On several occasions, I even had to insist to be accepted in this police. I was told there was no positions. I was invited to join the newly formed HVO Jure Francetic." And then after the next question, the soldier says, "We have fair and professional relationships. Everyone knows who is subordinate and superordinate to whom." And then this: "The orders that we receive from the brigade commander and from our platoon leader are carried out correctly, honourably, and honestly, and we try, within our abilities, to complete each task." He goes on to deal with the training. Isn't that the reality that military police were within the command of commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are presenting a document connected to the Jure Francetic HVO Brigade in Zenica and this weekly was published by the Zenica HVO so it has nothing to do with Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at this text more closely, I have the impression that this was a civilian policeman who had completed school in Sarajevo and then probably worked somewhere. I haven't read the entire text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Nice. What is being discussed here is whether the military police, as such, can somehow be regarded as an independent autonomous unit or entity. However, generally speaking, the military police are not autonomous in a military structure. Could the witness tell us as regards Vitez and what he has testified about whether the military police there was autonomous in relation to the military structure, in relation to the brigade? Is that what you are maintaining, sir, that is, that the military police was autonomous in regard to the brigade in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm saying, but perhaps it should be clarified that in Central Bosnia, there was the 4th Military Police Battalion, there were also the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, but at the level of the entire level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the military police command was not in Vitez. I don't know exactly what it was called. It was -- excuse me, it was somewhere in Herzegovina, whether in Mostar or Grude, I can't remember. That's where their main command was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the Vitez Military Police would receive their orders from where, exactly, if I got you right?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, mostly I think orders arrived through the Operative Zone, through the corps, because that was the highest level of command at that time in Central Bosnia and in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you speak about the 4th Battalion of the Military Police in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you say that the command of the military police was not located in Vitez. So what is the link between the Vitez Military Police and that battalion of the military police you mentioned? What is the connection between the two?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the same police. The entire military police in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was divided into battalions, that was the professional military police, and the 4th Battalion was in Central Bosnia. I don't know where the others were, on which territories, but they had their common command, and I'm not sure whether it was in Mostar or Grude, but it was somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You understand, don't you, Major, that the significance of all of this is as follows: If military police, whether from the brigade or whether called brigade military police or from the 4th Battalion were involved in Ahmici, and if they were in the command of Cerkez, then Cerkez will bear responsibility for them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not under the command of Cerkez. And that parts of the 4th Battalion were involved in Ahmici, well, that's something that I have already said that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you told us yesterday that although there were people called brigade military police, they weren't, in any sense, under the direct command of the commander of a brigade until August; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you're not really acknowledging any particular closeness between the 4th Brigade of the Military Police and the Viteska Brigade either in April of 1993 or at all, are you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can look at the next exhibit, 902.2, please. This is a document from -- only a draft translation at the moment, I'm afraid. It's from Blaskic, it's dated the 11th of May, and it is sent, I think, to the Vitez Forward Command Post. It's in respect of carrying out sabotage and ambush operations and it goes to the commander of the Vitez Brigade personally, to the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, Vitez, for information. And it says this: "Due to the intensification of activities by Muslim forces in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. area of the farm feature Divjak, and due to constant supply of MTS and fresh sources from Novi Travnik to Kruscica, and in order to prevent these activities, I hereby order ..." And then 1 is evaluation, 2 is "Contact the 4th Military Police Battalion and agree on engagement of members of the Jokers unit in executing the planned operation. Prepare and conduct the operation at the highest level of secrecy." Now, that's the way things operated, is it, with the 4th Military Police Battalion, that Blaskic would give an order to Cerkez and that people like the Jokers and the 4th Military Police would cooperate, fall into line, and do what they were told?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it's a little illogical, in item 2, that contact should be established with the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion and the Jokers. I think these are two separate units. But this is a normal way for things to be done. Why not? For this task, Blaskic could have issued an order to the commander of the Vitez Brigade to establish contact with the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police. Why not? And this was for the carrying out of this order. So the commander of the brigade could not have on his own initiative taken men from the military police unit without contacting their commander. So in this case alone, with Blaskic's command, he could have contacted the military police commander to reach an agreement with him not to issue an order to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He could have done exactly the same sort of thing on the night of the Ahmici massacre, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean he could have agreed with the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police on his own initiative? Do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He could have instructed Cerkez, whether in writing or otherwise, to contact, to agree with, and to act together with the 4th Military Police and the Jokers. This document shows how things happened, Major, doesn't it, when there were joint operations? It's as clear as daylight.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows how things were done in particular cases. This case is connected specifically to a certain operation and refers only to that operation and no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I accept that, in the same way as I'm going to ask you to accept that we haven't seen anything like all the orders that were issued on the night of the 15th, 16th. Do you accept that you haven't produced all the orders that must have been issued by Blaskic on the night of the 15th, 16th?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Where haven't I produced them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a matter of argument. I'll move on to the next document, and indeed I think the penultimate one in the series, 30th of May, Exhibit 997.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just -- it's not interruption of questioning. It's just for the record. We have never seen such documents, so we do not -- we cannot be sure whether it is truthful, whether it's authentic. We never saw it. And even I'm not sure whether this document is coming from current discoveries in Zagreb, because all the discoveries we are receiving from Zagreb are marked by the small stamp on the upper right corner with the words "national archives." So it could also be -- it could also be -- I'm not claiming that -- an earlier document in the possession which was not discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll clarify the position over the lunch adjournment and explain it to Mr. Kovacic, and we can raise it with the Chamber if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now then, Major, you see, you've told us, quite emphatically, that the document of August that you produced marks the opening day on which there were command -- on which there were brigade military police subject to the brigade's commander. This is a document dated the 30th of May of 1993. It comes from Blaskic. It's an order on the organisation of units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. It goes, as we can see, to the commanders of brigades 1 to 10. It also goes to -- and Vitez is, of course, mentioned there within the defence offices. It goes to the commanders of the independent units, various kinds, and to the military police battalions. And it reads: "An assessment of the situation regarding organisation of HVO units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and the quality of the command and control system in the units showed numerous weaknesses, resulting in duality of leadership and command, overlapping of authority, unauthorised combat operations without orders from a superior commander, insecurity among citizens in HVO-controlled areas, inability to prevent crime, and large numbers of HVO and civilian casualties. "In order to remedy these shortcomings I hereby issue the following order: All units in a brigade zone of responsibility are subordinate to the command and control of the brigade commander. The combat use of units in a brigade's zone of responsibility and the execution of combat operations is the exclusive jurisdiction of the brigade commanders who are personally responsible for Blaskic. Units which have been formed upon an initiative without an establishment decreed and approved by the Mostar defence department shall be immediately disbanded." Now, I don't know if I need read the rest. You must have been aware of this order, Major. It came in May of 1993. Were you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now. There were so many papers, so many orders. But this order is very clear. It is not clear to me what is not clear here. You have not asked me a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have. I've asked you if you were aware of this order, Major, because you produced a later one and I want to know why this one wasn't produced. Did you really not remember it or did you really not see it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because what it says is that things have to be made regular, and it makes it clear that all units are in the brigade commander's responsibility. Now, that's not what you told us yesterday, is it? Because you told us yesterday that military police, brigade and otherwise, were independent until August. Why did you tell us that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know -- you're not giving me enough time to explain, and it's evident that either you -- you are not aware of how things looked, how things were. So let's start from this order. An order saying that all units in the brigade zone of responsibility are subordinate to the command and control of the brigade commander is a framework order which I assert could never have been carried out, because certain units could never be put under the command of the brigade. First of all, the Vitezovi PPN, Special Purposes Unit, and the other units never permitted brigade commanders to issue them orders. There were even cases when there were conflicts between them and the commander of the corps and Colonel Blaskic when they openly refused to obey his orders. So -- excuse me -- there is -- there was no chance of putting these units under the command of the Vitez Brigade. This order means that when, with the permission -- or if it is so ordered by the superior command, if a brigade, in certain periods of time or in cases of fierce fighting, helps with some of their men, this order means that those men are put at the disposal, for a strictly limited period of time, of the brigade. They are helping. And that those men are then under the command of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major, you are asking us to believe that, are you? If that is what the order meant, why didn't it say so?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just said the order does say that all units are subordinate, but I'm saying that it could never have been carried out in practice, nor was it carried out as it's stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are trying to put a gloss upon the order and say that it was only for limited purposes. There is no mention of that in the order. Now, are you telling us the truth or not?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you the truth, because I know for certain what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, why didn't the order say what you say it meant?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why the order didn't say that, because an order can't say -- if it's a general order, you can't put exceptions in it and say that special units are exempt. I don't know why this was not stated in the order, but it wasn't stated, because all those units, those independent units, were supposed to be under the command of the corps. But I'm saying that at certain moments not even the corps commander could give them orders, because they were self-willed, let alone a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a different point as to whether the subordinates would obey the order. But the fact is that the words are quite straightforward, and you are trying to suggest that it means something different. I don't think we need debate the matter further. We'll adjourn now. We have again to take a longer adjournment, 3.00. Unfortunately, we have a meeting at 4.30, so we're going to be limited for time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help? I hope the Chamber will accept that the topics I've covered are pretty central to the issue. There's one other topic that's central, which I must deal with. I may make the decision, if it is acceptable to the Chamber, frankly to abandon matters of detail, like Mujezinovic and other named people, and leave those as matters for argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we'd be grateful if you would. Yes, 3.00, please. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just have, at most, four short documents on the same topic. First, 1116.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, Major, is an order of Cerkez dated the 27th of June, so before the date when you say there was command of the brigade military police. It's an order in respect of Private Matosevic who is being transferred from one company to another and under reasons, it says this, "The commander of the 2nd company issued an order to the Brigade Police to arrest Private Matosevic." Now, the commander of a company is plainly subordinate to Cerkez and here is a company commander recorded as issuing instructions to the brigade police because the brigade police were under Cerkez's command; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In your question you mentioned the 2nd army. What were you referring to actually? The 2nd army?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that must have been a translation error or alternatively a slip of my tongue for which I apologise. I think I was referring to a transfer from the 2nd to the 3rd Company.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just read this. In this order, one can see that the commander of the 2nd company asked -- requested the brigade to have Vjekoslav Matosevic -- just a minute, please. Yes, I'm reading the order. I don't think there's anything that should be contested here. Every commander, if he deemed it necessary to have a member of his battalion brought into custody, then he sent that to the brigade and he probably emphasised the brigade because he wanted to show what was involved because other requests were sent as well. However, the commander of the 2nd Battalion could not directly ask the military police to bring a soldier into custody. He could only do it through the brigade, and the brigade through the command of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police. And here it says in the upper part that this order will be carried out by the 2nd Battalion of the Viteska Brigade, that is to say, that he will carry this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you not accept and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just in order to clarify the situation and in accordance with earlier statements, there is definitely an error in translation. The key word in the lower part of the document in the first sentence is "request," and earlier the witness has told us what is the difference between request and the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where does "request" appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Croatian version, the word "request" is used not "order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it should read -- don't interrupt, please. It should read, should it, "The 2nd company requested an order;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The sentence should read, "The commander of the 2nd company issued a request to the brigade police to arrest private ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, it is not the 2nd Company; it is the 2nd Battalion. In the original it says battalion, bojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next exhibit, I'm sorry if there is a translation error. Let's move on to 1337A briefly. I can hand my document in to save time. If it can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, Major, is a December 1993 record, I think probably at the time you say you were making your archives recording deaths of the Viteska Brigade, and it's as clear as can be. We see within the brigade there's deaths one, two, three, four, five, associated with the brigade military police, all those deaths happening on the 18th of July of 1993. That is before the time when you say there was any brigade military police under the command of the Viteska Brigade. So please explain to us why there are these entries about deaths in July 1993 under brigade military police.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when I spoke about the classification and sorting of these archives, these documents, I was not the only person who was involved in this. I was involved least of all. Every one of us had things to do. However, since you are asking this question, I have already said that we called in the brigade military police because they were in the brigade as proof that -- at that time, these men who were killed in July, 1993, were under the command of their commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police is the fact that I remember well, the action when these men were killed. It was organised by the Operative Zone and it used parts of the military police for this action. These young men were temporarily in the brigade as the military police from the composition of the 4th Battalion but they did take part in this action, and they were killed during that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think that's your explanation for that document and we'll just then look briefly at your own document and turn to another topic. Your own document was D91/2. If I can have that document. This is a draft translation, so we better check on the tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the Chamber's leave, it may be worth putting the original on the ELMO and asking just the first sentence of paragraph one to be read by the witness out loud and translated for us by our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you be good enough, Major, please, to read from your own document, the first sentence of paragraph one, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The brigade military police is under the direct command of the brigade --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness will have to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you read it again, please, more slowly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The brigade military police is under the direct control of the brigade commander and it is situated in the establishment system of the brigade and has the same status as other units in the brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Major, this document which you've produced, I'm going to use words and if you don't follow them, I'll use other words. It is descriptive, it is not prescriptive. It is describing a state of affairs; it is not saying that that has to change. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. This document is describing the state of affairs. It's saying that the brigade military police is under the command of the brigade. It's not saying that it will be or that it should be; it's describing events as they were at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it describes events, and this order states specifically that from the day of the 18th of August, when this order was written, it will be within the composition of the brigade. And point 2 says that the commander can choose the persons he wishes to have, and he can make his choice only out of the manpower he already has.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that the document says no such thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting that the document says no such thing as "from the 18th of August"; it's simply saying that the police are under command of the commander, and that your interpretation of the document is incorrect, Major.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation is the correct one, as far as I'm concerned. But now, the word order in the sentence, I don't know. But in the order it says the date and the number and the hour when the order was issued, and it says that the brigade military police will be under the direct command of the brigade commander. If it had been that way before, then this order would have been pointless. It wouldn't have been necessary to repeat the same order ten times. So if it had been under the command of the brigade commander before, then this order would have been superfluous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move to two other topics, each of them fairly short. Before I come to them, two other questions, and I think that will be all I have to ask you. The first of the other questions is this: The man known as Bralo, you know who I mean by that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bralo? You are probably referring to a person whose nickname was Cicko; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. He was detained in Kaonik until the night of the 15th, 16th. Who had the power to release him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I know that he was at Kaonik. I don't know whether the judgement was already in the stage of sentencing, whether he had been sentenced. I think that it involved the killing of a neighbour or something. But I heard later that he was in prison. But who released him and on whose orders and who issued that order, that I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, are you telling us that despite all your listening to rumour and stories about Ahmici, you don't know or you haven't heard that Bralo was released from prison in order to take part in the Ahmici massacre?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I don't know that he was released. I mean, if he had not run away, if he had not escaped, then he was released, but I don't know who released him or who had the power to release him from prison at that point. Whether he was taken away at someone's initiative, I don't know really. With your permission, I did not have any contacts with the prison in Kaonik or -- I don't know. I know it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just the last question on this so that I can follow it. From all that you had heard about Ahmici from those few who, one way or another, were able to talk about what happened, did you hear the rumour that Bralo had been released and was engaged in the attack? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the rumour that he had been released, that I did not hear of; and that he participated, that I did hear of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what part did you hear he had taken, then? What had he done? Who had he led? Who had he killed? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he led anyone, because I thought he was a person who could not -- he was an unaccountable person. And what he did in Ahmici, I heard that again from rumour. Apparently he killed everything he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a little bit of the detail we've got from you. I think I asked you about detail probably earlier today. What other details by way of rumours did you hear about who killed whom in Ahmici, please, Major? Can you tell us about anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, what can the possible objection be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I object to that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The witness clearly said that he doesn't know any details, that what he heard was briefly rumours, and he said what he heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel is entitled to press him on a matter of this sort, to test his credibility, amongst other things. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Major, your initial evidence was that you heard a bit but you knew very little. When pressed about Bralo, it appears you heard quite a lot. Now tell us the rest that you heard, and in particular, who killed whom?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say who killed whom, nor do I know that, but this -- I know about Bralo, because this same Bralo, as he was walking around cafes and getting drunk, he talked about it himself. I'm not the only person who knows about this. Masses of people know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I want to know about some other people. What about Pasko Ljubicic? Do you know anything about him and what he did?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not one word, are you telling us that, bearing in mind you've taken a solemn affirmation -- declaration, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean -- you mean this oath that I took here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the fact that I'm speaking under oath, and I responsibly state that I do not know anything about what Pasko Ljubicic did. I said that at that time Pasko Ljubicic was most probably the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police. That I know. But what he did, I wasn't following that man, I was not in contact with him, we did not meet each other, we didn't talk, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. One other tiny matter of detail before I move to the only other two topics I'm going to trouble you with, Major. It's a tiny matter of detail. It may help us. Central Bosnia Operating Zone, what areas or municipalities did it cover?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, as far as I know, it covered Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, I think Kiseljak and Fojnica. But already after the 16th of April, they were cut off from the organic entity of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic is this: You've given an account of the development of the Viteska Brigade, and you're really trying to tell us, as I understand it, that it was only partly formed and small in size by the time of Ahmici. Would that be a fair summary of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The truth is that it was far more developed and probably larger than you've led the Judges to believe, and I'm suggesting to you that the only reason you could have for understating its size is to try and help Cerkez by the evidence that you're giving. So do you follow the suggestion I'm putting to you?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am following you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few documents, and there may be some others for argument later, but there's a couple of new -- a few new ones. 199.3 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, dated the 31st of August of 1992, from Blaskic, is an order improving the system of command, coordination and cooperation, identifying operating zones, indeed including Central Bosnia, so perhaps my last question was unnecessary, but making it clear that operational zones were to be identified at that stage. You accept that that was happening as early as August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm deeply sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not signed by Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not signed by Blaskic. Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is simply a matter of confusion, Your Honour. My dear colleague said that the document is produced by Blaskic. That is simply not the case. And that may confuse the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's difficult to see the signature. Do you know who it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's obvious from the -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's coming from the main headquarters. Quite right. It doesn't -- I withdraw that suggestion. In haste, or in speed, I'm probably going too fast. My fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But Major, the point is that here's an order, 31st of August, territorial responsibility for zones already being established; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. 292.2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I would like to ask the witness about what -- because here in -- we have a distinction between the Operative Zones which are four: South-east, north-west, Central Bosnia, and Posavina Operative Zone, OZ. And then we have in point two, the territorial responsibility of the Operative Zone, zone by zone. And in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Central Bosnia, we have as -- in Central Bosnia Operative Zone we have a territorial responsibility for Vitez. Vitez is described here as territorial responsibility inside the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. I would like to ask the witness what does it mean for him, as a military person, the territorial responsibility? What is the meaning of territorial responsibility for him as a military person?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, the territorial responsibility for these Operative Zones which are being set up, as far as I can see, is simply the word describing the area in which that particular Operative Zone operates. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to you, what is the responsibility of a commander who has some territorial responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a rather complex question, the responsibility of the commander, the responsibility of the commander in that area. Two things arise here, the territorial responsibility, I don't know, I tried to explain what -- how I understand it. But there is also the area of responsibility which is something completely different. Now, you are asking me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at all. What -- you see, within the framework of the Operative Zone, there are several people who have territorial responsibility. For instance, for Central Bosnia, you have Jajce, Donji Vakuf, Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Kiseljak, Zepce. And these are regarded as part of the territorial responsibility within the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. So please define for us what is the territorial responsibility of a commander? What does it mean? You were in the Viteska Brigade. The Viteska Brigade has a territorial responsibility over Vitez. What is the commander's responsibility? Who has territorial responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure whether I will be able to define the term "territorial responsibility" because I've never come across this term before. In military terminology, I never came across the term "teritorijalna obrana". I'm sorry, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to help you. Since you were a member of the Viteska Brigade, do you know whether, normally speaking, a commander must be aware of everything that happens on the territory which is under his command? Must he -- does he have to look after that territory? It is no longer simply hierarchical. It relates to a territory, to some space.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I believe we come to what I call the area of responsibility. That is the commander, his area of responsibility, an area in which his units conduct combat operations should be responsible for that. But how far each commander is the master of the situation in that particular territory, that is his business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But normally speaking, he must be aware of everything that is happening and he must take actions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, he should be abreast of everything that has to do with his formation, because he's a military man. And the principle subject of his concern is his formation, the situation in the formation, the strength of the unit, materiel, equipment, living conditions of his men, their equipment, the manner in which they conduct their operations, and so on. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So perhaps if we look at the next document to follow on perhaps His Honour's question in relation to that. The next document is 292.2. Now, this document dated the 25th of November does come from Blaskic and it now deals with, if we look at it, Major, the entire central Operative Zone, and I think and it breaks that area down, as we can see, into brigades which it says are to be organised in the following areas. And number three is the Novi Travnik and Vitez Brigade with its seat in Vitez. And under two, we can see that further reflected by the request or -- for proposals for a consolidated name for that brigade. Well, now, picking up the answers you were giving to His Honour just now, is not the reality that there was an overall responsibility for this entire zone falling on Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is logical that it be Blaskic because he was the commander of the Operative Zone except that here, under three, there is a mistake. There is an error here. It says, "Brigade Novi Travnik and Vitez with headquarters in Vitez," which is not correct. So it must have been either a typing error, because Novi Travnik and Vitez Brigade with the headquarters in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's the document. But in any event, by the 25th of November, it was clear that there was organisation of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone dividing it up into brigades as set out here; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operative Zone, according to this document, was divided into administrative subdivisions, that is, municipalities and every municipality was to have its own brigade except that Vitez and Novi Travnik created one brigade with the exception of municipalities where there were no Croats from which they had been expelled. So that we have the Jajce Brigade with its headquarters in the Travnik barracks under nine, but I simply do not recall this brigade. As far as I know, members of these formations -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to trouble you about Jajce. I want to now focus down on to the joint brigade that was formed, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, and that brigade had been a long time in the preparation, hadn't it? It had been being prepared and recruited for what, for months already by November?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that this was being prepared. I didn't know that the preparations for the establishment of Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade for months. I do not know when it was decided to form that brigade, but it was a very short period of time before we left to Novi Travnik and set up the command there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, again, to save time, there's a document you can look at if you like, but I'm going to make a suggestion to you and see if you accept it. The Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade had a 2nd Battalion and it was that 2nd Battalion that became the Viteska Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, yes. Later on it became part of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you accept -- and there's a document which is simply a list of names, and they can all be counted and they have been -- would you accept that on the 27th of February of 1993, the 2nd Battalion of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade already numbered 433 men or maybe men and women, but certainly 433 soldiers? Would you accept that? The document is Z505. And if you don't accept it, of course you can have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't accept the figure because, as I've told you, we never had that many soldiers in one place. When you say a battalion and you think that you have 300 armed men and ready to engage in combat operations at any time, the 2nd Battalion from Vitez is a reserve force from the list of this battalion which covered the population from all parts of the municipality and who were called up in shifts and sent to do their shifts over ten days or something. They would come back home, and then they stopped being soldiers. Now, how many men passed through this list, I cannot say, but this figure is much too high.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it? Well, I'm not going to count the figures at the moment. That can always be done later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can the witness now please see 562.1, and while that's coming to you, what would your understanding be -- no, just a minute. Sorry, a mistake there in the documents. I'll have to come back to that but I'm not going to take time. Can we have 557.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the 20th of March of 1993, Cerkez, pursuant to an order given by the command and reforming of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade into two brigades, requested a complete list of men of military age from Vitez in order to provide a complete system and records of those included in the units. Interestingly enough, he copied the document to the 4th Battalion of the regional police. But by the 20th of March, things had reached this degree of sophistication, hadn't they, getting complete lists of men in Vitez? Correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand it was a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, my mistake. I'm trying to move too fast. By this date, the 20th of March, the preparation for this part of the brigade, which was to become the Viteska Brigade, was already seeking information on all men from Vitez of military age. Was this an advanced state of preparation?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not an advanced stage of the preparations; this is one of the initial stages. Because with this order, Mr. Mario Cerkez is requesting simply the lists from the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, the civilian police, and so on so forth to see what men are engaged in those units in order to be able to count on other men because he cannot request demobilisation of those men if they already have their combat assignments in these units. So he simply wanted to go through those lists to screen them, to sieve them, so as to know not to have to call them up since they were already engaged with those units not to issue double summons or be unable to mobilise them later on and -- so things like that. And hence this order -- rather, this is not an order, this is -- this is a letter in which he is asking for all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to the document I was hoping to show you earlier. It's 516.2, already produced. I'll make mine available to save time. Original for the witness, English version for the ELMO. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This much is right, isn't it, that as early as the 1st of March of 1993, there was a demand for the immediate formation of a brigade of Vitez municipality, with the following organisational form: One battalion of -- and I emphasise this -- active-duty personnel; and two battalions of the Home Guard. What did you understand by "active-duty personnel," if it wasn't trained and existing soldiers, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, they are far from being trained or professional soldiers. It was all -- there were all sorts of people in the municipality. This battalion of active-duty personnel -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What does "active duty personnel" mean as opposed to battalions of the Home Guard, as you've been attempting to say, really, that the Viteska Brigade is a sort of Home Guard unit. What's the difference between these two parts, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, some thoughts were aired -- I don't know. It was said that perhaps such an active-duty formation could be set up, that is, to have certain men who would become part of it would be getting some kind of remuneration. I don't know. It would make part of their seniority or their years of service, something of the sort. Because the Viteska Brigade was all made of Home Guard men; there were no professional soldiers. This term, "active duty," was used, but there was no active-duty formation, no special active-duty formation, then or ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's have a look at 562.1. And if I can have the other document back. This Home Guard Brigade that was being formed on the 23rd of March of 1993 was already planning for its own Security Service, wasn't it? It may seem a small point, but in view of what you're saying, this Home Guard Battalion has got its own Security Service, it being established, by this document, on the 23rd of March, because they want furniture for them and fittings. Can you explain that for your Home Guard unit, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing to explain. In the brigade formation, there is also the Security Service and the Military Intelligence Service, according to the formation, that is, according to the book which prescribes the number, the type, and the kind of the personnel, and of course those people have to work for the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember this morning when I asked you who would be the person most able to help us with what Cerkez was doing and you reeled off half a dozen or more deputies? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you sure you're not attempting to understate the sophistication and state of readiness of this brigade, Major?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am positive. Not only that I'm not trying to understate it; I'm simply trying to tell you what it really looked like, and that is what I'm sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 570.1, please. Sorry, 570.2. And if it will help the Chamber and my learned friends, on this exercise I've only got I think about one more document to deal with, and then I've got a very short further exercise, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 26th of March of 1993, Cerkez sends this letter: "On the basis of operations, files, and documents for all MTS in Vitez, we've come across the following information: Many of our members of the Vitez Brigade, and also those of the Home Guard, have guns that are out of service because there is no ammunition for them." So the first point is: Contrary to what you're telling the Chamber, there seems to be a distinction, even in Cerkez's mind, and as early as March 1993, between his brigade and the Home Guard. Please explain that to us, Major.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are trying all the time to tell us that we should think that the Vitez Brigade was a particularly well-trained and equipped formation of the army and that they all had their high-ranking officers and so on and so forth. You must understand that under the circumstances, when the Vitez Brigade was formed, we were all in a way -- no, not in a way. We had all come from some other civilian jobs to join the army. We do not have a proper military vocabulary, we are not familiar with military terms, or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to answer my question, please. What is the distinction --

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what Mr. Cerkez meant by this, but to my mind, there was no difference, unless he perhaps meant Home Guard, that those were only those village guards which used to exist before, but they had not yet become a part of the formation until the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then let's look at the next sentence. He says of the brigade and of the Home Guard that they have guns that are out of service because there's no ammunition for them. And he then says: "It's indicative that this is the case with a large number of guns, approximately 500 pieces of various types," and he lists them. Are you going to suggest that each member of the Home -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you going to suggest that each member of the Home Guard, or many of them, had more than one gun, or does these 500 guns, which can only be part of the brigade in the Home Guard, that these 500 guns reveal as a reality there's rather more than 500 men already signed up in one way or another? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, this document says that there are more barrels, but the men did not have those barrels. That is, there were less men than barrels. And these barrels mostly come from the Slimena depot and I think they were stored in our depot, but they practically could not be used because we lacked ammunition for them. However, we counted on them, and when we eventually obtained ammunition for them, that then we would issue them to the men of the Vitez Brigade, of course, if we could get the ammunition for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you accept that at the time of the writing of this letter, there must have been, frankly, at least 500 men in what was the Viteska Brigade? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what do you say was your rate of recruitment, approximately, per week or per month in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not easy to answer that, because I was not involved in these matters, and I couldn't really give you any more exact explanation of what the rate was. I know that my colleagues from the department for organisation and personnel were looking around enterprises for lists of the former employees in former formations and were trying to compile some lists which could then be used for mobilisation purposes. But that was for some kind of keeping record. But at the end of the story, of course, the mobilisation was a matter for the defence office.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then let's look at your own exhibit, very briefly, D87/2. And if the Chamber looks at the second sheet in English, this is a document dated the 24th of April, from the Vitez Brigade. And the second sheet deals with Defence Sector 1, signed by Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you, Major, can see this at the foot of the first page and onto the second. And what we can see here, if we look at the second sheet of the first page, the third paragraph: "At the time of maximum combat readiness, there are 244 defenders on the sectors line of defence," and that's Defence Sector 1. If the usher would be good enough and we can turn to the next sheet, we can see at the top of the page Defence Sector 2's figure, about six lines down, which is 120 defenders. If we cast our eyes down to the bottom of our screen, Defence Sector 3 is 190 defenders. If the usher would be good enough to turn over to the next page, please. Defence Sector 4, about a third of the way down the screen, 160 men. And Defence Sector 5, we can see just at the bottom of the screen, 160 men. Total number of men, 874. Is that about right for the number of men actually engaged, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that number, but you will allow that the date is the 24th of April. You were asking me about March. This is a month later. And then the conflict had already started and our Home Guards were joined by the village patrols and others, which is why the number grew. But a month before that day, it couldn't have been 500 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I've asked you about the rate of recruitment and you were unable to help me. That's why I asked you. Can we turn to the next issue -- I don't know what time the Court is sitting to this afternoon. It's about three documents on this exercise. You've been asked about a man called Marko Lujic and you tell us something about him. Just in summary, what is it you want to tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to say anything. I was just answering the question of the Defence as to whether I knew Mr. Marko Lujic, and I said yes. Whether he was the chief of the artillery in the Vitez Brigade, I answered no. There was nothing special I wanted to say about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say he had nothing to do with the Viteska Brigade at all?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that he was not a member of the command of the Vitez Brigade and he was not a soldier. He was not a member of the Vitez Brigade. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was he, then? You tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that in Princip, that is, the enterprise, he was the director of wartime production. What his exact duty was, I don't know. I didn't go into it. But I know he was involved in wartime production and he was some kind of director or chief boss, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware of evidence about an intercepted call between him and Cerkez on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the suggestion that he's not a member or never was a member of the Viteska Brigade, can the witness have Exhibit 2480.2. I think that's already in. Sorry. I'm so sorry not to have given notice, if we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, if you'd like to have the original, please. The English is in two pages. The first page, recommendation for an award, refers to Marko Lujic, son of a man of the same first name, and it says then, under paragraph 3: "In the reserve since the 16th of April of 1993." If we then turn to the second page -- and I hope you'll be able to follow this in the original -- under paragraph 8, details of duties, subparagraph B, says this: "Member of the army of the Republic of Croatia July 1991 to the end of the same year. Logistics support for HR and HB armed forces in Croatia until the 1st of March, 1992. Carried out the same duties in the area of Vitez municipality in Central Bosnia, as a member of the HVO, from March 1992 to the 16th of April, 1993." And then this: "Member of the Vitez Brigade units working on missile systems from the 16th of April, 1993 to the 1st of August, 1993. Chief of war production from the 1st of August." Absolutely nothing inconsistent, is there, between what is revealed about this man and his firing weapons on the 16th of April? He was in the Vitez Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document which you have just presented, there are many such documents, and it confirms that Marko Lujic was a member of the Vitez Brigade. I am certain, however, that this was written only so that he could be given a certain rank. But I assert again, as far as I'm concerned, Marko Lujic was never a member of the Vitez Brigade. I don't know if ever I saw him in the command throughout the conflict. I'm not sure I ever saw him in the command, nor did I ever see him in any unit of the Vitez Brigade, never. And if you were to ask all the survivors, all the surviving members of the Vitez Brigade, I guarantee that every one of them would say the same thing. That's one point. Another point is that the Vitez Brigade did not have any rocket systems. Where would we get rocket systems?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look, please, at this page, which has been prepared by the chief of the defence office, or prepared for him to sign, and it sets out, quite specifically, working on missile systems from the 16th of April, 1993, to the 1st of August. And the evidence that's been given in this Court is of an overheard conversation between him and Cerkez about firing rockets or other projectiles at religious objects in Kruscica. The evidence suggests that this man asked for a break so that he could have breakfast. Can you explain, please, why simply to give someone a rank, you're going to prepare a document falsely stating "working on missile systems," especially if, as you're trying to tell us, there weren't any available to the Viteska Brigade? Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to apologise. When I talked about missile systems, I was referring to real missile systems, so to speak, that is, missile systems which were in use in the JNA before that, you understand; those that, according to the establishment, belonged to certain units. It's another question if you are referring to the small guns and entire fire equipment. These were not real missile systems. And I assert that we did not have any missile systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just get this quite clear, Major. You were at home on your sick bed on the 16th of April, and you can't provide any evidence to suggest that this man, Lujic, was not firing guns at the religious objects in Kruscica to Cerkez's order, can you? You can't provide any evidence to counter that.

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot offer any evidence that Lujic did not fire out of those -- out of that equipment, nor can I prove that this was in agreement with Mr. Cerkez, of course. Whether it was Marko Lujic who did that, I do not know, and I do not know on whose orders, if he did, he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to bother with the other exhibits that may relate to this topic. There's a link exhibit, 2480.3. And literally the last document and my last question, a slightly different topic and then I'm done, it's 1147.4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slightly different topic, Major. Sorry to change -- the last change and the last question. This is the 20th of July of 1993. It's an order from Blaskic and it's an order in respect of one of the special purposes unit, on this occasion the Vitezovi. And it says: "Send a strengthened platoon to help regain the broken line. It doesn't matter where." And then it says this: "The unit will be subordinated to the Vitez Brigade commander and will remain so until the task is carried out." To achieve coordination of activity in your area, from time to time special units were subordinated to your commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this order was written by Franjo Nakic. Franjo Nakic worked for a long time in the manoeuvring units in the JNA, and he wrote this from a purely military point of view. There were cases when Viteska Brigade was helped by the PPNs, the Vitezovi and others. I don't know which ones, which ones are there. It says here that they would be attached during the duration of that task, but once this task is over, then they would be returned to where they came from. That is what the order clearly says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Don't overlook the fact that at the top it says rejected and not carried out, but I think you answered my question by agreement. Sometimes special purpose units were indeed subordinated to Cerkez. A simple answer to that question is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I said that there were cases when special purpose units did come to help the Viteska Brigade. However, these same units would leave the positions whenever they wanted to and in any way they wanted to. Even General Blaskic could not have stopped them. I was personally a witness of things like that happening on several occasions. So commanding them is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got about five minutes. Will that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that may be just about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sajevic, I know it's late, I know you are exhausted already. We all are. But please concentrate for another few minutes. I am going to put some very clear and concise questions to you and try to answer them as briefly as possible in a word or two. My first question is the following: Is it correct that every brigade in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia had its own established zone of responsibility at least on the 16th of April when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZELJKO SAJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
